draft.title: The opening of Japan
card: From the 1630s, Japan's Tokugawa shoguns (military rulers) strictly limited contact with the outside world. Only a few Dutch and Chinese traders were allowed, at Nagasaki. This near isolation lasted about two centuries.
In 1853 an American naval commander, Commodore Matthew Perry, sailed warships into Edo Bay. He carried a letter from the US president asking Japan to open its ports to trade.

Japan's rulers knew that Western ships and guns were far stronger than their own. Fearing defeat, they gave in. In 1854 they signed a treaty opening some ports to American ships, and more treaties with other powers followed.
The treaties ended Japan's isolation. Many Japanese were angry that the shogun had given way to foreign pressure, and this anger weakened his rule.
draft.remember: Perry's warships in 1853 pressured Japan into opening its ports, ending about two centuries of near isolation.

a.q: Why did Japan's rulers agree to open their ports after Perry arrived in 1853?
opts: They feared the Western warships were too strong to resist
They wanted Japan to stop trading with the Dutch and Chinese
They had already built a modern army and navy of their own
They were asked politely and had no fear of foreign power
a.why: Japan's rulers saw that Western ships and guns were stronger than their own, so they gave in rather than risk defeat. They did not have a modern army yet, so the option about a modern army is wrong.
a.clue: Think about how Japan's military compared with Perry's ships.

b.q: A student says the shogun's government chose to open Japan freely, with no pressure from outside. Which fact from 1853 to 1854 best shows the student is wrong?
opts: Perry sailed warships into Edo Bay before the treaty
Dutch and Chinese traders were allowed at Nagasaki
The 1854 treaty opened only some ports to ships
Many Japanese were angry at the treaties once signed
b.why: Warships arriving before the treaty shows the threat of force behind the request. The Nagasaki trade and the limit to some ports are true, but they do not show pressure. Anger at the treaties came after they were signed, so it does not show how the decision was made.
b.clue: Look for the fact that shows force was present before the signing.

wants.brief: A Japanese woodblock print or other period artwork from the 1850s showing Commodore Perry's American warships in Edo Bay, open licence.
wants.why: Seeing the large Western ships helps students understand why Japan's rulers felt unable to resist.

b.best: Perry sailed warships into Edo Bay before the treaty
